paragraphs: A photo can capture a meaningful moment while still having an awkward viewpoint, composition, or pose. The paper introduces Aesthetic Photo Reconstruction as the task of correcting this structure while retaining the subject’s identity and the scene’s meaning. This requires more than making an edit that looks plausible: the system must decide which structural changes would improve the photograph.

AesFormer separates that decision from carrying out the edit. Its first component, AesThinker, examines the image through seven photographic dimensions and produces actions an editor can execute. The authors additionally use GRPO-A to encourage exploration of different action plans beyond supervised fine-tuning. A second component, AesEditor, then performs structural changes conditioned on those actions.

The work also introduces a pipeline for mining examples from video and an evaluation benchmark, AesRecon, containing 9,071 closely aligned poor-and-good image pairs. Experiments report substantial improvements on the reconstruction task and competitive performance with Nano Banana Pro. The findings support explicitly planning aesthetic changes before asking an image model to execute them.
icml-2026-aesformer-transform-everyday-p.tldr: AesFormer plans aesthetic improvements before editing photo structure, improving reconstruction while aiming to preserve identity and scene meaning.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse asks what changes to a person’s attributes could produce a more favorable model decision. The paper examines this question for tabular predictions made through in-context learning, where a language model receives labeled examples at prediction time instead of undergoing explicit task training. This creates a setting in which the examples supplied to the model are part of the decision process.

The authors analyze whether recourse remains mathematically well-defined in this setting. They establish boundedness and characterize how solutions approach classical recourse solutions as the number of contextual examples increases. This connects recourse for in-context prediction to an existing body of methods while describing how context size affects that connection.

Their practical method, ASR-ICL, searches for recourse without requiring model gradients or access to internal parameters. It produces actionable changes involving relatively few features and extends to tasks with multiple classes. Across real-world datasets and models, it achieves comparable recourse quality with fewer model queries. Experiments also exhibit the convergence behavior predicted by the analysis.
icml-2026-algorithmic-recourse-of-in-con.tldr: ASR-ICL generates sparse, actionable recourse for black-box in-context predictors, with theoretical and empirical links to classical recourse.

paragraphs: Biomedical signals can vary between people even when they correspond to the same label. BioFormer addresses the challenge of learning patterns that transfer to unseen subjects by explicitly describing part of this variation in frequency space. The authors call it spectral drift: signals often retain similar oscillatory structure while particular frequency components differ in magnitude or phase across subjects.

The model’s Frequency-Band Alignment Module uses the signal’s spectral distribution to generate adjustments for individual frequency bands. These adjustments modify amplitude and phase to bring spectral structures into closer alignment. This gives the model a direct mechanism for reducing the subject-dependent variation identified by the authors, rather than relying only on the rest of the network to suppress it implicitly.

BioFormer also derives normalization parameters from each signal’s own statistics instead of subject identity. This complements frequency alignment by stabilizing representations across people. Across six datasets, the paper reports performance above 12 baselines, with absolute F1-score improvements of 6%. These results support explicitly modeling spectral variation as a useful route to cross-subject generalization.
icml-2026-bioformer-rethinking-cross-sub.tldr: BioFormer improves cross-subject biomedical prediction by aligning frequency structure and normalizing signals using their intrinsic statistics.

paragraphs: An improvement after training can mean that a language model learned a new capability or became better at using knowledge it already possessed. This paper investigates that distinction by measuring how much generalizable information training adds. Its central finding is that eliciting an existing capability can require dramatically less information than teaching a capability to a comparable performance level.

The authors use excess description length, or EDL, to quantify that information. They find different EDL patterns for elicitation and teaching as the information supplied during learning increases. In many elicitation cases, just a few bits contained in one example unlock a large fraction of the model’s maximum performance. This is a reported pattern across cases, rather than a claim that every capability can be unlocked so cheaply.

EDL also estimates how much predictive information a model can compress into its trainable parameters. The resulting capacity estimates describe tradeoffs between data quantity and parameter count. The authors show that these tradeoffs robustly predict when parameter-efficient approaches such as LoRA underperform full fine-tuning, connecting learning mechanisms to practical adaptation choices.
icml-2026-bits-that-count-quantifying-an.tldr: An information measure distinguishes eliciting existing capabilities from teaching new ones and predicts when parameter-efficient fine-tuning falls short.

paragraphs: The paper asks how one fake-image detector can work across four forensic subdomains. Although a single model is presented as theoretically promising, such models have performed worse in practice than ensemble approaches. The authors attribute this problem to the distinct kinds of artifacts found in different subdomains, a difference they name the Ji-Zhe phenomenon.

Their diagnosis is that combining these tasks can collapse the artifact feature space: the representation loses distinctions needed for detection. The desired representation must therefore support shared detection while retaining differences among artifact types. The authors hypothesize that high-level semantic information can supply structure for rebuilding this space, and introduce Semantic-Induced Constrained Adaptation, or SICA, around that idea.

On the authors’ OpenMMSec dataset, SICA outperforms 15 state-of-the-art methods. Their experiments also show a reconstructed artifact space with a near-orthogonal organization, supporting the proposed role of semantic structure. The significance is that unified detection need not depend on merging all artifact information into an indistinct representation; the reported approach preserves discriminative structure within one model.
icml-2026-can-we-build-a-monolithic-mode.tldr: SICA uses semantic structure to help one fake-image detector preserve distinct artifact features across four forensic subdomains.

paragraphs: The reversal curse occurs when a model learns a fact in one direction but struggles to recover the inverse relation. This paper studies the problem through internal representations, describing an asymmetry between latent states organized around subjects and those organized around objects. That perspective shifts attention toward how stored representations can be accessed during a reverse query.

The proposed Chiral Transformer uses contrastive regularization to encourage a structured mapping between these states. The mapping is intended to be involutive, meaning that applying it twice returns to the starting representation. At inference, Adjoint-Induced Retrieval uses the learned map to read out model-derived entity representations. The evaluated procedure is therefore a structured retrieval setting, rather than unrestricted autoregressive answer generation.

Experiments on inverse-relation benchmarks show substantial improvements in inverse factual access, including 65.07% accuracy on Fact-Inv-300. These findings support the possibility that some inverse relations are difficult to retrieve because ordinary readout fails to expose useful latent structure. They do not establish that missing training data is irrelevant or that unrestricted generation has solved the reversal curse.
icml-2026-chiral-symmetry-breaking-in-tr.tldr: A learned symmetry-aware mapping improves inverse-fact retrieval, supporting a representation-access explanation for part of the reversal curse.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with coverage guarantees when calibration and deployment data satisfy exchangeability. This paper studies a transfer setting where that relationship fails: labels exist only in a source space, but predictions are needed in a different target space. Unlabeled observations paired across the two spaces provide the connection, as can occur with different modalities or sensors.

Transported Conformal Calibration first uses those pairs to move labeled source calibration into the target space. It then corrects remaining mismatch using unlabeled target inputs. TCC-KS uses a label-free uncertainty signal to detect mismatch and adjust calibration conservatively. The alternative, weighted-TCC, reweights transported examples toward the target domain and improves efficiency when those weights are stable.

The authors provide finite-sample target coverage guarantees that adapt to an observable measure of mismatch. Experiments on CIFAR-100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C, and SEN12MS demonstrate reliable coverage transfer without labeled target calibration examples. Label-free diagnostics also predict when correction is needed, making residual mismatch something the procedure can assess and respond to.
icml-2026-conformal-calibration-transfer.tldr: Transported Conformal Calibration transfers prediction-set calibration through unlabeled pairs and corrects residual target mismatch without target labels.

paragraphs: DNA investigates whether pretrained models already contain features useful for detecting realistic generated images. The authors propose extracting this latent detection capability instead of relying on extensive end-to-end fine-tuning. Their approach searches within a model for units sensitive to forgery traces, with the aim of separating those signals from the broader semantic information the model represents.

The search proceeds from layers to individual units. First, the framework analyzes feature separation and changes in attention to locate intermediate layers where the model’s focus shifts from overall semantics toward local anomalies. It then combines a three-part scoring rule with curvature-based truncation to remove semantic redundancy and isolate forgery-discriminative units. These selected units serve as the framework’s discriminative neural anchors.

The paper also introduces HIFI-Gen, a benchmark of high-fidelity synthetic images from recent generators. Experiments report superior detection using the anchors alone, including few-shot conditions, and robustness across architectures and previously unseen generators. The results support extracting existing forgery-sensitive features as an effective alternative to extensive fine-tuning in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-dna-uncovering-universal-laten.tldr: DNA isolates forgery-sensitive units already present in pretrained models and reports strong detection with limited examples and unseen generators.

paragraphs: Small benchmarks and stochastic model outputs can make accuracy estimates noisy enough to change model rankings. This paper draws on an additional signal: even when a model cannot solve a difficult problem, it may still judge which of two candidate solutions is better. Such comparisons can carry useful evaluation information beyond whether the final generated answer is correct.

The framework combines ordinary labeled outcomes with judgments of auxiliary reasoning chains. It treats comparison signals as control variates, using them to reduce noise in performance estimation. For the setting where those auxiliary chains are observed, the authors derive a one-step estimator through an efficient influence function. They establish the semiparametric efficiency bound, strict variance reduction relative to simple averaging, and asymptotic normality for uncertainty quantification.

Simulations show better ranking accuracy, with larger gains as output noise increases. Experiments on GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, and GSM8K also yield more precise estimates and more reliable rankings, especially with small samples. The contribution improves how existing evaluation evidence is used; the comparisons supplement labeled correctness outcomes.
icml-2026-evaluating-llms-when-they-do-n.tldr: Combining answer correctness with pairwise solution judgments yields lower-variance performance estimates and more reliable model rankings.

paragraphs: Kernel regression offers strong statistical tools, but computations that grow cubically with sample count make large datasets difficult to handle. This paper introduces a framework with O(n log n) complexity and a design suited to GPU acceleration. It represents kernels in Fourier space and uses non-uniform fast Fourier transforms to perform the required computations quickly and with reduced memory use.

The authors develop versions for Sobolev kernel regression, physics-informed regression, and additive models. They show that the estimators achieve minimax convergence rates, preserving the statistical guarantees associated with classical kernel theory. Empirical results report processing datasets containing up to tens of billions of samples within minutes, demonstrating the scale possible in the supported settings.

The computational benefits depend on efficiently expressing the kernel norm in Fourier space and having a small ambient dimension. Although the theory applies in all dimensions, the implemented Sobolev package relies on CufiNUFFT, whose cost grows exponentially with dimension and currently restricts it to at most three dimensions. The additive implementation likewise supports simple effects without interactions.
icml-2026-fast-kernel-methods-sobolev-ph.tldr: Fourier-based kernel regression achieves O(n log n) scaling and statistical guarantees, with current implementations constrained to low-dimensional settings.

paragraphs: Federated learning must accommodate clients whose data and available computing resources differ. A client model needs knowledge suited to its own data as well as knowledge that transfers across clients. This paper argues that personalization suffers when these two kinds of knowledge become entangled or when either one dominates the other.

FedEMoE separates their roles through an Elastic Mixture of Experts architecture. Personalized experts extract features at multiple scales to enrich client-specific knowledge. An elastic shared expert handles transferable knowledge across heterogeneous client models. Its capacity can expand or shrink according to expert status, assessed through analysis of the spectrum of model weights, addressing a bottleneck in transferring shared knowledge.

The resulting design makes personalization and generalization distinct architectural responsibilities while allowing shared capacity to adapt. Experiments cover differences in both client data distributions and model architectures. Across diverse datasets, the authors report significantly higher accuracy for the heterogeneous models than state-of-the-art methods. These findings support separating specialized and shared knowledge when clients cannot all use the same model or learn from similarly distributed data.
icml-2026-fedemoe-improving-personalizat.tldr: FedEMoE improves heterogeneous federated learning by separating personalized experts from an adaptively sized shared expert.

paragraphs: Numerical prediction becomes difficult when target values follow a long-tailed distribution: common values dominate training while rare values receive less attention. The paper finds that multimodal language models trained with token-level supervision or rewards for individual predictions tend toward the mean and perform poorly in the tails. It identifies missing supervision about relationships between examples as a key contributor.

The proposed framework adds that relational information through reinforcement learning based on Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its reward uses the Concordance Correlation Coefficient to compare predictions and ground truth across a batch. This signal accounts for correlation, scale, and mean, encouraging the collection of predictions to match more of the target distribution’s structure.

The method requires no change to the model architecture, making the intervention a change in training supervision. On a unified collection of long-tailed regression benchmarks, it consistently improves over supervised fine-tuning and existing multimodal regression methods. Gains are particularly strong in medium- and few-shot regimes. The findings support evaluating predictions jointly across examples when isolated prediction rewards encourage excessive concentration around common targets.
icml-2026-injecting-distributional-aware.tldr: A batch-level distribution-aware reward improves multimodal numerical regression under long-tailed targets without changing model architecture.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can represent rich action distributions for reinforcement learning, but generating actions through repeated refinement creates substantial overhead. Mean Flow Policy Optimization replaces this policy representation with MeanFlow, a class of generative models designed to produce samples in few steps. The aim is to retain an expressive policy while reducing the cost of both learning and action generation.

The method trains these policies within maximum entropy reinforcement learning, which promotes exploration alongside reward seeking. It uses soft policy iteration and addresses two difficulties that arise for MeanFlow policies: evaluating action likelihoods and carrying out soft policy improvement. These are necessary parts of making the chosen generative representation work within this optimization framework.

Experiments cover MuJoCo, the DeepMind Control Suite, and HumanoidBench. The authors report performance comparable to or above current diffusion-based baselines while substantially reducing training and inference time. This suggests that the long iterative sampling process of diffusion policies is not required to obtain their level of control performance on the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2026-mean-flow-policy-optimization-.tldr: Mean Flow Policy Optimization uses few-step generative policies to match or exceed diffusion-based control performance with less computation.

paragraphs: A discrete distribution can contain several likely regions separated by high-energy barriers. Neural samplers may concentrate on only some of these regions and miss the configurations between them. That omission matters for tasks such as reconstructing free energy and studying phase transitions, where access to barrier regions is part of the scientific objective.

MetaDNS adds well-tempered metadynamics to discrete diffusion or autoregressive samplers. It maintains an adaptive bias potential along selected low-dimensional coordinates, updating that bias using sampling history. This actively encourages exploration of regions the sampler previously failed to reach. The resulting high-energy samples enable free-energy reconstruction that standard neural samplers cannot perform when those samples are absent.

The authors evaluate the framework on low-temperature Ising, Potts, and copper-gold binary alloy benchmarks. MetaDNS reproduces the thermodynamic distribution in these experiments. It also achieves exploration comparable to MCMC-based metadynamics with fewer bias deposition steps. The findings show that adapting the exploration landscape can address missing regions in neural sampling while supporting the thermodynamic quantities the samples are intended to reveal.
icml-2026-metadns-enhancing-exploration-.tldr: MetaDNS adds history-dependent exploration bias to discrete neural samplers, enabling barrier-region sampling and free-energy reconstruction.

paragraphs: Learning a successful policy from human preferences and identifying a broadly accurate reward function are different objectives. A policy may only need reward accuracy in the states and actions it encounters. This paper instead studies compatible reward identification: finding reward functions consistent with observed preferences and accurate across the entire state-action space, motivated by transferability, safety, and interpretability.

For deterministic preferences, the authors derive the minimum number of interactions required to identify the set of compatible rewards. They also show that using fewer queries can lead to arbitrarily large suboptimality. This gives a theoretical reason why preference elicitation adequate for a narrower policy-learning objective may be insufficient for comprehensive reward identification.

The paper then considers stochastic preferences modeled by Bradley-Terry. It introduces a query basis and an associated index to describe problem complexity, studies their relationship to that preference model, and discusses limitations the model creates in this setting. An algorithm identifies a nearly optimal query basis using polynomially many human queries. The result connects which comparisons to request with the broader reward information those comparisons must establish.
icml-2026-online-compatible-reward-ident.tldr: The paper characterizes preference-query requirements for identifying broadly accurate compatible rewards and develops an efficient query-basis algorithm.

paragraphs: Generating a chain of thought one token at a time can encourage locally plausible steps without a reliable overall plan. The paper connects this lack of global guidance to redundant or inaccurate reasoning. It proposes PTA-GRPO, a two-stage training framework that develops compact planning guidance alongside the detailed reasoning used to reach an answer.

In the first stage, a language model summarizes chains of thought into high-level guidance. Those summaries then support supervised fine-tuning. The second stage introduces guidance-aware reinforcement learning that jointly optimizes final outputs and the quality of the guidance. This makes the usefulness of the plan part of the training objective, alongside the eventual result of following it.

The authors evaluate the framework on ten mathematics and natural-science reasoning benchmarks, using five base models spanning multiple modalities. They report consistent, stable, and significant improvements across models and tasks. These results support teaching models to organize reasoning at both planning and detailed execution levels, with the reported generalization grounded in the range of evaluated models and benchmarks.
icml-2026-plan-then-action-high-level-pl.tldr: PTA-GRPO trains high-level plans and detailed reasoning together, improving results across the tested models and reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Controlling what a discrete diffusion model generates can require expensive computation or additional training. Gradient-Informed Logit Correction, or GILC, offers a way to guide a pretrained model toward a reward without retraining it. The paper evaluates this idea in settings where outputs include DNA, protein sequences, and molecules.

GILC reuses the pretrained denoising network as a variational proxy for estimating guidance signals. To avoid gradient instability in high-dimensional discrete spaces, it directly adjusts the logits for the clean prediction through a Jacobian-free mechanism. These logits determine the model’s preferences among discrete output choices, so correcting them provides a point at which guidance can influence generation.

The framework supports both differentiable rewards and rewards that do not provide gradients. Experiments across the three application areas report state-of-the-art performance without additional training, frequently exceeding fine-tuning approaches. The findings indicate that a pretrained denoiser can supply useful guidance information as well as generate samples, allowing control to be introduced through its predictions instead of requiring a newly trained model for each objective.
icml-2026-plug-and-play-guidance-for-dis.tldr: GILC guides discrete diffusion generation by correcting prediction logits, supporting varied rewards without additional training.

paragraphs: Flow-based policies can represent flexible action distributions, but optimizing them for high value is difficult. A direct gradient approach must backpropagate through the numerical solver that generates actions, which can create instability. Existing methods often respond by limiting policy expressiveness, leaving a tradeoff between representing complex behavior and training reliably.

Q-Flow uses the deterministic dynamics of the flow to assign terminal trajectory value to intermediate latent states. Those intermediate states then provide value gradients for policy optimization. This avoids unrolling the numerical solver during the update and gives the framework a way to improve the policy without imposing the same restrictions on representational flexibility.

On the OGBench suite in offline reinforcement learning, Q-Flow consistently exceeds state-of-the-art baselines, with an average advantage of 10.6 percentage points. The framework also supports stable online adaptation. Together, these findings suggest that moving value information inside the policy’s generative trajectory can make its expressiveness easier to optimize, both when learning from existing data and when subsequently adapting through interaction.
icml-2026-q-flow-stable-and-expressive-r.tldr: Q-Flow propagates value to intermediate flow states, enabling stable policy optimization without backpropagating through an unrolled numerical solver.

paragraphs: Language models generate probabilistically, so their behavior includes events that are unusual but potentially consequential. Such events are hard to observe during development precisely because they happen infrequently. The paper emphasizes that large deployment volumes change their practical importance: behavior absent from development observations can become prominent when a model is used at enormous scale.

The authors present an end-to-end framework for analyzing these events systematically. It connects theoretical foundations with efficient strategies for generating rare behavior, estimating its probability, and analyzing estimation error. Bringing these pieces together matters because producing an unusual example and understanding how often it occurs are separate parts of the analysis.

A practical implementation and concrete examples illustrate the framework. The paper also outlines extensions to other models and contexts, presenting the concepts as more broadly applicable than the immediate language-model setting. Its contribution is a connected methodology for investigating the tails of model behavior, including uncertainty in probability estimates, rather than relying only on the behaviors most readily observed in ordinary use.
icml-2026-rare-event-analysis-of-large-l.tldr: The paper provides a practical framework for generating, measuring, and analyzing uncertainty around rare language-model behavior.

paragraphs: Vision foundation models provide features rich in semantic information, but their size and redundancy can make diffusion transformers harder to train efficiently. RePack then Refine separates the useful structural information in those features from the detail needed in the final image. The framework organizes generation around a compact representation and restores fine detail afterward.

First, RePack projects high-dimensional features onto a low-dimensional space, removing redundancy while preserving essential structure. A standard diffusion transformer learns to generate within that compressed space. Because compression loses some high-frequency information, a Latent-Guided Refiner is trained last to enhance image details. The three stages assign compact generative modeling and detail recovery to separate components.

On ImageNet-1K, RePack-DiT-XL/1 reaches an FID of 1.82 after 64 training epochs. Adding the refiner improves that value to 1.65. The authors report substantially better convergence efficiency than recent latent diffusion models. These results support compression followed by targeted refinement as a practical way to balance image fidelity against the training burden of rich foundation-model features.
icml-2026-repack-then-refine-efficient-d.tldr: RePack then Refine trains diffusion transformers on compact semantic features and restores fine details afterward, improving convergence efficiency.

paragraphs: Language-model-based speech systems can produce expressive audio, but controlling emotion in an interpretable way remains difficult. This paper examines the semantic hidden states inside these systems using sparse autoencoders. The goal is to identify a sparse set of latent features through which emotional variation can be understood and deliberately influenced.

The analysis finds that emotional variation is distributed across several features, while modifying a small subset can provide useful control. Building on that finding, the authors introduce interventions that can both induce and suppress emotion without changing the backbone model’s parameters. This places control at the level of selected internal features rather than requiring a global change to the entire activation representation.

Distinct features are associated with particular acoustic attributes, including pitch. These associations suggest that emotional expression emerges from coordinated contributions across features. Experiments show emotion induction and suppression comparable to or better than global steering and existing text-to-speech baselines. The work therefore links a more inspectable representation of emotion with an effective means of changing the generated speech.
icml-2026-sparse-autoencoders-for-interp.tldr: Sparse autoencoders reveal internal speech features that enable interpretable emotion induction and suppression without modifying backbone parameters.

paragraphs: Proximal Policy Optimization can be sensitive to how its policy and value networks change during training. SPPO addresses this through a drop-in augmentation that retains PPO’s clipped objective and network architecture. It focuses on the internal representations and update directions of the actor and critic, along with the incentives that encourage exploration.

Three mechanisms work together: a CKA-based constraint on critic representations, a no-flip regularizer for actor updates, and kernel-density-based advantage shaping. The theoretical analysis links these mechanisms to tighter bounds on one-step bootstrapping error, improved expected alignment of action-update directions, and non-decreasing occupancy mass in highly novel regions. These are specific properties of the analyzed mechanisms, rather than a general guarantee of monotonically improving returns.

Experiments on standard continuous-control benchmarks show consistent gains over PPO and recent stabilization approaches. Ablations measure the individual contributions and complementary effects of the three components. Analyses of training dynamics also show fewer oscillations and less instability in actor and critic updates, connecting the reported performance gains to more stable learning behavior.
icml-2026-stabilizing-ppo-via-latent-spa.tldr: SPPO improves PPO stability through critic constraints, actor update regularization, and novelty-aware advantage shaping.

paragraphs: Watermarking embeds ownership information in a model so that unauthorized use can be investigated. This paper focuses on graph neural networks and the problems of backdoor-based watermarks, which manipulate training data. Such methods can make ownership claims ambiguous through misclassification and can depend on data mechanisms vulnerable to poisoning.

The proposed method embeds a watermark in the model’s explanations, making them statistically distinguishable from other explanations. Verification therefore requires a statistically significant ownership signal. The approach retains black-box verification while avoiding training-data manipulation, which the authors identify as removing the associated ownership ambiguity and data dependencies.

The paper proves that locating the watermark is NP-hard even when the method itself is fully known. This is a computational hardness result, rather than a statement that discovery is impossible in every instance. Experiments additionally show robustness against fine-tuning and pruning attacks. Together, the theory and experiments support explanations as a carrier of ownership information that can be checked externally and can survive the tested model modifications.
icml-2026-watermarking-graph-neural-netw.tldr: The method watermarks graph neural network explanations for statistical ownership verification and shows robustness to fine-tuning and pruning.

paragraphs: Long reasoning sequences require models to retain information during generation, making their key-value caches costly but difficult to compress safely. Dropping tokens can remove intermediate reasoning information, while head-allocation strategies developed for retrieval may overlook heads that preserve reasoning consistency or help determine when generation should stop.

RLKV uses reinforcement learning to investigate which attention heads matter for actual generation outcomes. It optimizes their cache usage against reasoning quality, turning compression decisions into a probe of head importance. The resulting strategy keeps full caches for reasoning-critical heads and assigns aggressively compressed, constant-size caches to the others.

Experiments find that a fraction of heads is essential for reasoning across the tested tasks and models. This enables cache reductions of 20–60% with near-lossless performance, and up to a 2.06-fold end-to-end speedup at 60% reduction. The findings support allocating memory according to a head’s demonstrated contribution to reasoning, with the reported preservation of performance remaining near-lossless rather than an exact guarantee of unchanged outputs.
icml-2026-which-heads-matter-for-reasoni.tldr: RLKV learns which attention heads need full memory, enabling 20–60% cache reduction with near-lossless reasoning performance.

paragraphs: The computational difficulty of neural-network training depends partly on how numbers are represented. Traditional analyses often use a model that operates directly on real numbers. This paper instead studies empirical risk minimization when inputs and parameters are rational numbers with polynomially bounded bit lengths, bringing finite numerical representation into the complexity question.

Under this bit-level model, activation functions create a sharp divide. For deep networks with rational-coefficient polynomial activations of degree at least two, deciding the training problem is #P-hard. Determining a particular gradient bit is also #P-hard, and even determining the sign of one partial derivative is unlikely to admit an efficient randomized algorithm.

For piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, the training decision problem is NP-complete, while standard backpropagation takes polynomial time and precision requirements remain manageable. NP-completeness still leaves optimization computationally difficult in general. The distinction is that ReLU permits efficient gradient computation in this model, whereas polynomial activations can make even gradient information computationally hard. Finite precision thus changes the theoretical comparison between activation families.
icml-2026-why-relu-a-bit-model-dichotomy.tldr: A finite-bit analysis shows that ReLU permits polynomial-time backpropagation while polynomial activations can make even gradient computation hard.
